01.title: Who helps keep a website safe?
01.question: What do security companies actually do?
01.idea: Imagine you run an online shop. You can buy tools that watch it, hire people to watch those tools, or hire someone to try breaking in with your permission.
steps: You have a website, customer accounts and orders.
Software spots something unusual, such as lots of failed sign-ins.
Someone investigates. Is this an attack, or a customer who forgot a password?
The person allowed to act decides whether to block access.
Confirm the unwanted access stopped. Check that customers can still shop.
01.caption: One possible way a security service works. Each company and contract divides the jobs differently.
explain: Think of a security product as an alarm. A managed service adds people who watch the alarm. An assessment is an agreed investigation into how someone might get in.
The research looked at ten providers, including Microsoft, CrowdStrike and Japanese firms. It followed their public descriptions of who notices a problem, who makes decisions and who can act.

contrast.right: We checked the device and confirmed the unwanted access stopped.

01.recall: You bought an alarm for your shop. What job still needs a person?
01.answer: Someone must decide what an alert means, decide what to do, and check that the response worked. Some services do parts of this for you; the agreement matters.

example.title: Three things you might buy
example.prompt: Pick one to see the job it does.

options.label: A product
options.headline: “Tell me when something looks unusual.”
options.body: Like buying an alarm. Your team still needs to configure it and decide what to do when it rings.

options.label: A managed service
options.headline: “Have someone watch and investigate.”
options.body: Like hiring an alarm-monitoring team. Which actions they can take depends on the service and your agreement.
options.result: You get people operating agreed capabilities.

options.label: An assessment
options.headline: “Find out how someone could get in.”
options.body: You agree on what may be tested. Specialists investigate and explain what they found and how to fix it.
options.result: You get answers to an agreed question.

02.title: How do people look for weak spots?
02.question: What is a scan? What is a pentest?
02.idea: Your shop might let one customer read another customer's order. A security test asks whether that can happen—and collects enough evidence to explain the answer.
steps: Use accounts and orders that belong to the test.
Ask for Bob's order while signed in as Alice.
Did Alice receive Bob's private order details?
After the repair, check that Alice is refused and Bob can still see his own order.
02.caption: A made-up example for learning. The research used controlled local examples; this is not a test of a real shop.
explain: A scan runs a set of automated checks. A penetration test, often shortened to pentest, adds investigation into particular weak spots. A red-team exercise can ask whether the people defending a company notice and handle an agreed simulated attack.
We researched the tools, the public processes of testing companies, and small tests with known answers. We learned why counting warnings does not tell you how thoroughly a website was checked.

contrast.left: The tool says this page might expose private data.
contrast.right: In the agreed test, Alice actually received Bob's private order.

02.recall: A scan found no problems. Does that mean every customer account is safe?
02.answer: We still need to know what the scan checked, which accounts it used, and what it could not reach. It may never have tried the Alice/Bob example.

options.label: Scan
options.headline: “Do our automatic checks spot anything?”
options.body: The tool checks the pages and settings it can reach. Its checks may miss the rule that Alice must never see Bob's order.

options.label: Pentest
options.headline: “Can Alice actually read Bob's order?”
options.body: A tester investigates the agreed question using the two accounts, then records what happened.

options.label: Red team
options.headline: “Would our defenders notice and respond?”
options.body: An agreed exercise follows a simulated attack toward a goal, observing what the defending team sees and does.
options.result: Evidence about an agreed attack path and response.

03.title: What do all these tools let us see?
03.question: Why is there more than one security tool?
03.idea: When you press “View order,” your browser sends a message to the shop. Different tools let us inspect different parts of that exchange.
steps: Alice presses “View order” in her browser.
The browser asks the shop for an order.
The reply contains order data or a refusal.
A saved record lets us inspect the exchange later.
We ask whose order came back, and whether Alice was allowed to see it.
03.caption: Arrows show the order of this teaching example. Real tools can observe different parts, and saved copies may leave things out.
explain: A proxy is a go-between that can show messages between a browser and a website. A packet viewer shows pieces of network traffic. A discovery tool checks which systems answer from where you are.
The research followed how tools receive, change, save and display information. One lesson: a saved report is a copy with choices made along the way. Important details can be changed or left out.

contrast.left: The website replied with a particular set of data.
contrast.right: A tool saved and summarized that reply. We need to know which details survived.

03.recall: A report shows “request succeeded.” What would you inspect next?
03.answer: The actual request and reply, which account made it, and what data came back. The short label does not tell the whole story.

example.title: Follow a message into a report
example.prompt: Look at the detail that each view keeps.

options.label: The message
options.headline: “Alice asks for order 42.”
options.body: The record says which account asked, which order it requested, and what the website returned.
options.result: Keep the account and the returned data together.

options.label: A short report
options.headline: “One request succeeded.”
options.body: That summary has dropped the most important question: was order 42 Alice's, or someone else's?
options.result: A shorter record can lose the reason the result matters.

04.title: A network address is not a person
04.question: What do VPNs and proxies change?
04.idea: Two customers can share one internet address, just as two people can live at one street address. Changing the route to a shop does not change which account you are signed into.
steps: Alice and Bob use the same café Wi-Fi.
To the shop, their traffic can appear to come from the same internet address.
A VPN or proxy can carry selected traffic through another system.
Alice should still see only Alice's orders, whichever route she uses.
04.caption: A simplified example. Which traffic uses a VPN or proxy depends on the actual setup.
explain: A VPN can carry traffic through an encrypted connection to another system. A proxy carries selected requests on your behalf. They change the path and who can observe parts of it.
They do not automatically give you permission to enter a website or see someone else's data. Our research separated network routing from accounts and permissions.

contrast.left: The shop sees the café's internet address.
contrast.right: The shop checks Alice's account before returning private data.

04.recall: If a shop blocks the café's address, who might lose access?
04.answer: Other people sharing that address, including legitimate customers. An address alone is an imperfect way to tell people apart.

example.title: Two people, one café
example.prompt: Compare what the shop can infer.

options.label: Same Wi-Fi
options.headline: One address. Two accounts.
options.body: Alice and Bob can share the café's public address while signing into completely different customer accounts.
options.result: A shared address does not mean a shared person.

options.label: Alice uses a VPN
options.headline: New route. Still Alice's account.
options.body: Some traffic now travels through the VPN. Alice is still signed in as Alice; the shop still needs to check which orders she may read.
options.result: A changed address does not grant new account permissions.

05.title: How do lots of automatic workers cooperate?
05.question: What happens when a job is retried or cancelled?
05.idea: Imagine several workers generating receipts for your shop. They need a shared to-do list so they know what to do, who is doing it, and what happened if someone stops replying.
steps: The shared list says “create a receipt for order 42.”
One worker gets temporary ownership of the job.
The worker stops replying. Another worker may be asked to retry.
Did the first receipt already get created? Repeating the job could create a duplicate.
05.caption: A fictional receipt job. It illustrates a failure pattern discussed in the worker and queue research.
explain: A queue is a shared list of jobs. A worker is a program that takes a job and does it. Temporary ownership is often called a lease: it can expire if the worker does not renew it.
We studied queues, retries and cancellation. A central lesson is that sending “stop” and confirming the work has stopped are different events.

contrast.left: The cancellation request reached the worker.
contrast.right: We checked that the worker has finished stopping and is no longer doing the relevant work.

05.recall: Why could retrying a job make a second receipt?
05.answer: The first worker may have created the receipt before losing contact. The shared list may know the worker stopped replying without knowing the receipt already exists.

example.title: What does “cancelled” mean?
example.prompt: Follow the difference between a request and its effect.

options.label: Stop requested
options.headline: The worker receives “please stop.”
options.body: A cooperative worker checks the signal and stops. A worker that ignores it may continue.
options.result: We know a signal was sent.

options.label: Stop checked
options.headline: We check that work is no longer continuing.
options.body: We wait for the relevant task to settle and inspect its result. Any work already done still needs to be accounted for.
options.result: We have evidence about what actually stopped.

06.title: When should you believe a result?
06.question: What does a green PASS actually tell us?
06.idea: A test can pass while checking the wrong thing. Before trusting “PASS,” ask what question the test actually answered.
steps: Alice must not be able to read Bob's order.
Make the request while signed in as Alice.
Read the returned data, including any private details.
Did Bob's order reach Alice? That decides this test's result.
Record what was tested. Other pages, accounts and cases may still be untested.
06.caption: This is a teaching example of choosing a meaningful check. Passing this one test would not prove the whole shop is safe.
explain: A status code is a website's short response label, such as 200 for success or 403 for refusal. The body of the reply is the actual content. A label saying “refused” is no help if private data is still included.
We researched how tools decide whether tests pass. The technical word for that decision rule is an oracle. You can read it as “the check used to decide the answer.”

contrast.left: “The website said access was refused, so PASS.”
contrast.right: “Alice did not receive Bob's private data, and the test actually reached the right page.”

06.recall: A page says “access denied” but includes Bob's address. Did the privacy rule hold?
06.answer: No. The reply gave Alice private data. The label and the actual content disagree.

example.title: The label can hide the problem
example.prompt: Which check answers the privacy question?

options.label: Read the label
options.headline: “403 — access denied.”
options.body: A test looking only at the short status label might treat this as a correct refusal.
options.result: We still do not know whether private data leaked.

options.label: Read the data
options.headline: Bob's address is inside the reply.
options.body: Alice received the private information despite the refusal label. The privacy rule failed in this example.
options.result: The actual returned data answers the question.

07.title: What changes when AI can take actions?
07.question: How is an AI suggestion different from an AI doing something?
07.idea: An AI can suggest blocking an account. If it also has a tool that can block accounts, we need to control when it may use that tool—and check the result.
steps: The assistant receives an alert and supporting information.
It proposes blocking a suspicious account.
Code checks what this assistant is allowed to do, and whether approval is required.
The permitted tool asks the shop to block the account.
A separate check asks whether that account is actually blocked.
07.caption: A conceptual example. It does not claim that a particular provider follows this exact flow.
explain: An agent is an AI system that can choose steps and use tools. The word does not tell you which tools it has or what it is allowed to do.
The research followed how selected agents use tools, save their progress and recover after problems. We also studied provider documents describing approvals and action results.

contrast.left: The assistant writes “the account is blocked.”
contrast.right: The shop's actual state confirms the intended account is blocked.

07.recall: Is writing “never block without approval” in a prompt enough?
07.answer: A prompt tells the model what it should do. A permission check in the action path controls what the tool can actually do. The research treats those as separate boundaries.

example.title: Advice and action need different controls
example.prompt: Choose what the assistant can do.

options.label: Give advice
options.headline: “I suggest blocking this account.”
options.body: A person can review the suggestion. The text itself has not changed the account.

options.label: Use a tool
options.headline: “Request a block through an allowed tool.”
options.body: Permissions and any required approval must be checked. A successful request still needs a check of the actual account state.
options.result: An action may occur; verify its effect.

08.title: How do we know a fix worked?
08.question: Is closing a report the same as fixing a problem?
08.idea: Suppose Alice could read Bob's order. After changing the website, repeat that test and check both customers: Alice must be refused, and Bob must still be able to read his own order.
steps: The agreed test shows Alice received Bob's order.
Did monitoring record the activity? Did anyone get an alert?
Someone investigates and chooses a response.
Repair the website's check of who may read the order.
Confirm Alice is refused and Bob's normal access still works.
08.caption: A possible investigation and repair sequence. The research does not establish that this entire sequence ran in a customer environment.
explain: A report can mark a problem “closed” because it was fixed, but also because it was not seen again or was filtered out. The status alone does not explain which happened.
Our research connects the original problem to a repeatable check. This makes it easier to ask whether the website improved, rather than only whether the report changed.

contrast.left: The problem is no longer listed as open.
contrast.right: The relevant test ran again and showed that the intended rule now holds.

08.recall: If the scanner could not log in, could a missing finding mean the site was repaired?
08.answer: We cannot tell from the missing finding. First check that collection worked and the relevant page was reached. Then test the repaired rule.

example.title: A useful before-and-after check
example.prompt: Compare these two ways of calling a problem fixed.

options.label: Report disappears
options.headline: “No finding in the new report.”
options.body: Perhaps the site was repaired. Perhaps the test never reached the order page. We need to know which.
options.result: Missing information leaves the repair uncertain.

options.label: Test repeats
options.headline: “Alice is refused. Bob can see his order.”
options.body: The test reached the correct page with both accounts and checked the intended privacy rule after the change.
